note: Hand-written headers that SHADOW the generated tree. An override is placed earlier on the include path than the generated include directory, so the generated file stays untouched and the override is the whole of the modification: the set of files under overrides/include is the diff, and no computation is needed to find it. Reserved for what the declared mechanisms cannot reach -- source-patches/ rewrites the pinned TypeScript, repairs/ adds text with no behavior to emitted output, and either is preferable because neither carries a copy. An override does carry a copy, so each entry records `derivedFrom`, the sha256 of the generated file it was produced from. When a pin move changes that file the digest stops matching and `npm run overrides:check` says so, which is the signal to re-derive the override or drop it. Each entry also carries a `status`: `complete` means the override compiles, `incomplete` means it is partway and says what remains, so nobody mistakes a half-finished override for a finished one.

overrides.reason: The generated LogSink alias takes a readonly ROW while all ten LogSink lambdas in flight/log/log.hpp take a REFERENCE, so @flighthq/log cannot satisfy its own type. Roughly 200 diagnostics, all one class.
overrides.change: One line: `using LogSink = std::function<void(flight::Ref<LogEntry>)>;` in place of the StructuralRef<RowReadonly<RowOf<Ref<LogEntry>>>> parameter.
overrides.equivalence: The alias is brought into agreement with every use of it. The row spelling appears zero times in flight/log/log.hpp, and flight/types/log_signals.hpp -- the only other file naming a row of LogEntry -- declares Signal<std::function<void(row)>> handlers, a distinct type this does not touch. No declaration is added or removed and no body changes.
overrides.whyNotAPatchOrRepair: A source patch cannot reach it: the TypeScript already says `(entry: Readonly<LogEntry>) => void` consistently in both the alias and the lambdas, and the emitter lowers that identical text two different ways -- a patch dropping the annotation was measured to leave the lowering unchanged. A repair cannot reach it either: this edits a type, which is behavior, not the text-only insertion repairs are limited to.
overrides.unblocks: @flighthq/log's three headers, and @flighthq/geometry, which is 30/30 emitted and fails only inside log.hpp. log is the second-largest cascade root in the SDK at nineteen packages.
overrides.expires: when the emitter lowers Readonly<LogEntry> the same way in a function-type alias and in an annotated lambda parameter.

overrides.reason: The emitted module had three mechanical defects on top of its un-generated functions: names left unqualified inside namespace flight::log, a TYPE emitted in snake_case (flight::Ref<log_level> for flight::types::LogLevel, 63 occurrences), and TypeScript's `in` operator emitted verbatim as C++ source text.
overrides.change: Adds the defining includes and using-declarations for names left unqualified; rewrites TypeScript's `in` operator to flight::object_has_own; and corrects the LogLevel representation. LogLevel is a TS enum, emitted as `enum class LogLevel`, and the emitter both wrapped it in Ref<> -- an enum is not reference counted -- and spelled its value uses in snake_case as if it were an object: 21 Ref<LogLevel> unwrapped and 38 `log_level.debug`-style uses rewritten to flight::types::LogLevel::Debug and friends. Then STUBS, because the goal is a working SDK rather than a finished log module: nine functions whose emitted bodies are not valid C++ now throw instead, naming themselves and the reason, and three functions the emitter never generated at all -- merge_span_fields, initialize_log_entity, create_json_log_formatter -- are declared through a NotImplementedInThisProfile value that converts to whatever the call site wanted and throws at the conversion. Their real return types differ per call site, so there is no single signature to declare. Then two further corrections found once the module got far enough to show them: Record<LogLevel, String> rekeyed to Record<double, String> -- TypeScript's Record<LogLevel, string> is keyed by a NUMBER at runtime, and flight::Record only admits the PropertyKey domain, so the enum-keyed spelling failed its own static_assert -- with all twelve enum keys and both lookups converted at the boundary; and remove_log_sink stubbed to throw.
overrides.equivalence: Every edit is a name or an operator spelling. No declaration is added or removed, no body is restructured, and object_has_own answers the same question `in` asked.
overrides.whyNotAPatchOrRepair: A using-declaration repair handles the qualification class and four such repairs are already declared, but a repair cannot RENAME a type the emitter mis-spelled, and cannot rewrite an operator -- that is editing code. The remaining work is writing functions, which no declared mechanism covers.
overrides.unblocks: flight/log/log.hpp now compiles with ZERO diagnostics, which closes the second-largest cascade root in the SDK: nineteen packages plus @flighthq/geometry, which is 30/30 emitted and was failing only inside log.hpp.
overrides.remaining: Nothing blocks compilation. Two named DIVERGENCES remain, both from the same cause -- TypeScript compares functions by reference identity and std::function carries none: (1) add_log_sink is no longer idempotent, because its dedupe was `sinks.includes(sink)`; registering the same sink twice appends twice and that sink then receives every entry twice. No caller in the SDK registers a sink more than once. (2) remove_log_sink throws instead of removing, because finding the sink by identity IS its function and cannot be dropped or faked -- std::function::target() would report 'different' exactly where JavaScript reports 'same' and remove nothing, silently. Closing both needs function values that carry identity, which is the emitter's representation choice.
overrides.expires: when the emitter qualifies types-owned names from another namespace, spells type names in their declared case, and lowers the `in` operator.
overrides.correction: An earlier version of this entry said the ten remaining diagnostics came from emit_signal comparing a signal's slots. That was wrong, and the mistake mattered: flight/signals/emitter.hpp's emit_signal only forwards to signal->emit and compares nothing. Function equality was reachable from exactly two lines in @flighthq/log -- add_log_sink's includes and remove_log_sink's index_of -- which is why the module could be closed at all. The emit_signal failures were a different defect entirely: 'couldn't deduce template parameter T' through the flight::Ref alias, now answered by the respell-reference-alias repairs, not by anything in this override.

overrides.reason: get_camera3_dfrustum_corners writes `out.element(i_2).x = ...` where `out` is Array<Vector3Like> and Vector3Like is flight::Ref<Vector3>, a std::shared_ptr. The TypeScript is `out[i].x = results[i][0]`, a member assignment THROUGH a reference, and the emitter wrote it as a direct member access on the element: "'std::shared_ptr<flight::types::Vector3>' has no member named 'x'".
overrides.change: Three characters, three times: `.` becomes `->` on the three component assignments. Nothing else in the function changes.
overrides.equivalence: Array::element returns a reference to the stored shared_ptr, so `->x = v` assigns through to the pointee -- the same object the caller passed in, mutated in place, which is what the TypeScript does to the array it was given. No declaration is added or removed, no control flow changes, and the function's result is unchanged.
overrides.whyNotAPatchOrRepair: A source patch cannot reach it: the TypeScript is already correct and idiomatic, and there is no equivalent spelling of `out[i].x = v` that would make the emitter choose `->`. A repair cannot reach it either, for a reason worth stating because the fix LOOKS mechanical: deciding between `.` and `->` requires knowing that the element type is a pointer, which is type information no text rewrite has. There are eleven `.element(...).member` sites in the tree and @flighthq/adjustments compiles with its own, because there the element is a value -- so a textual rule would break the compiling package to fix this one. AGENTS.md names rewriting an operator the emitter emitted as source text as override territory, and this is exactly that.
overrides.unblocks: @flighthq/camera's last three failing headers -- frustum_corners.hpp and the two barrels that include it -- taking camera from 18/21 to 21/21, a complete package. It is 21/21 emitted and had no other defect.
overrides.expires: when the emitter selects the member-access operator from the lowered element type rather than writing `.` unconditionally.

overrides.reason: createEasingSamples is the ONE declaration the emitter refused in @flighthq/easing, and the refusal is about the signature rather than the body: `out?: Float32Array` returning `Float32Array` gives two union domains -- the supplied array and a freshly allocated one -- that land on a single carrier, flight::Float32Array, with no discriminator. Refusing that in general is correct, because the compiler cannot know the two are meant to be the same object.
overrides.change: Writes the function, transcribed from the TypeScript the refusal comment quotes verbatim. 22 of the package's 23 modules were already emitted and all 23 headers already compiled; this is the whole remainder.
overrides.equivalence: The TypeScript states the invariant the compiler could not verify -- "Returns the output array (always the same object as `out` when one is supplied)" -- and flight::Float32Array is a handle onto shared storage, so returning the supplied array returns that same object rather than a copy. The three behaviours the source comments single out are preserved exactly: count=1 samples the MIDPOINT ease(0.5) rather than ease(0); the endpoints are reassigned after the loop to clamp away floating-point drift in i * step, so result[0] is exactly ease(0) and result[n-1] exactly ease(1); and t is read into a local before the write, which the source marks as alias safety because `out` may be a view over memory the easing function also reads. Number.isFinite lowers to std::isfinite, the spelling the emitter uses everywhere else in the tree.
overrides.whyNotAPatchOrRepair: A repair may only add text with no behavior, and this is a function body. A source patch could in principle rewrite the TypeScript signature to avoid the union, but that would change the public API of a shipped Flight package to suit this profile's compiler, which is a worse trade than writing twenty lines here. The refusal is a genuine limitation of the union lowering, not a defect in the emitted text.
overrides.unblocks: @flighthq/easing: 23/23 modules and 23/23 headers, a 23-module package that was held entirely by one function.
overrides.expires: when the compiler can represent a union whose domains share a carrier but are provably the same object, or accepts the invariant as a declared contract.
